opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest shift for me was realizing that a lot of what we used to call "capability limits" were really something else. Early on, when a model failed at a task, the instinct was to say, well, it's not smart enough yet, we need a bigger model or more pretraining. And sometimes that's true. But once you start scaling reinforcement learning seriously, you see that if you can define the task well and give the model a reliable signal for whether it succeeded, it gets remarkably good, remarkably fast. Competitive programming and math were the clearest examples. Those domains went from "models are kind of bad at this" to "models are among the best in the world" in a pretty short window.

So the question becomes: why doesn't that same thing happen everywhere? And what I came to believe is that the bottleneck in the real world is mostly not raw intelligence. It's things like: can you even specify what success looks like? Is the feedback clear, or is it delayed and noisy? Does the task need context that lives in someone's head, or in a codebase the model has never seen, or in an organization's unwritten norms? Real work is long-horizon, it's messy, the goals shift halfway through, and nobody hands you a grader at the end.

The other thing that became really apparent is robustness and reliability over long sequences of actions. A model can be brilliant on each individual step, but if it's ninety-five percent reliable per step and the task takes fifty steps, you're in trouble. Recovering from mistakes, noticing when you're stuck, knowing when to ask for help: those are skills, and they need to be trained just as deliberately as solving a hard math problem.

So my mental model changed from "we need smarter models" to "we need to bring real-world tasks into a form where learning can actually happen." That means better environments, better ways of giving feedback on fuzzy outcomes, and training models to operate over much longer horizons. The intelligence is increasingly there. The hard part is building the bridge between that intelligence and the messiness of actual work.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest shift for me was realizing that the bottleneck mostly wasn't the algorithm. When I started, I had this picture where reinforcement learning was the hard part, and if we just got the RL right, the models would start doing useful things. What actually happened, over and over, was that the RL worked fine and the thing that broke was everything around it.

Concretely, three things kept showing up.

The first was the reward. In a game like Dota or in a math competition, you know when you've won. Real tasks don't come with that. If you ask a model to fix a bug in a codebase, what counts as fixed? The tests pass, but did it break something the tests don't cover? Did it do it the way a human would accept in review? I spent a lot of time thinking I was doing RL research and was actually doing evaluation design, and I've come to think that's the honest description of most of the work. If you can measure it reliably, RL will climb it. The scarce thing is a reliable measurement.

The second was the environment. People underrate how much of the difficulty of a real task lives in the interaction loop rather than in the reasoning. The model has to run something, look at the output, decide the output was unexpected, and recover. Early on our models were surprisingly good at thinking about a problem and surprisingly bad at the mundane act of checking their work. And you don't get that from more pretraining. You get it by putting the model in a loop where it actually has to live with the consequences of its guesses. Building those loops at scale, with real tools and real failure modes, was a much bigger engineering project than I expected.

The third was that a lot of what looked like a capability gap was really a horizon problem. The model could do each step of a long task, but something went wrong at step forty and it couldn't get back on track. Scaling RL taught me that the ability to persist, notice you're stuck, and try something different is itself a learned skill, and it's one that only shows up when you train on tasks long enough for getting stuck to happen. Short tasks never teach it.

So the summary of the update is something like: I used to think the missing piece was intelligence, and now I think it's mostly contact with reality. The models already know a great deal. What stops them from solving real tasks is that they haven't had enough chances to act, be wrong, and find out. And the whole stack of reward, environments, and long-horizon training is really just machinery for giving them those chances.

astra-6.text:
The distinction I’d draw is between a model having a capability and being able to use it reliably. A model might solve a problem once, but a real-world task requires it to make a whole sequence of good decisions, recognize when something went wrong, and recover.

Reinforcement learning puts the feedback problem at the center of that. What are we rewarding? Can we actually tell whether the task was completed? In a setting where you can check the answer, you have a clear signal. In a more open-ended task, success can be ambiguous, and a response that looks convincing may still fail to accomplish what the user wanted.

So I’d frame the bottleneck as more than intelligence alone. It’s also the quality of the learning environment and the feedback, and whether those reward the behavior we actually need. Getting a successful attempt is one milestone. Getting dependable performance across unfamiliar situations is a much bigger one.

sol-6.1.text:
It changed my intuition about the gap between knowing something and being able to do it reliably. A model can explain how to solve a problem, but completing a real task means making a sequence of decisions, noticing when something goes wrong, and recovering. A small error early on can derail everything that follows.

Reinforcement learning gives you a way to train that behavior, but then the question becomes: what can you actually reward? For a math problem or a piece of code, you can often check the answer. For a real-world task, success can be ambiguous, the feedback can be delayed, and the environment can change while you’re working. If your reward captures only a proxy for success, the model can get better at that proxy without becoming more useful.

So I came to think of the bottleneck as more than model capability. It’s also our ability to build environments where models can practice meaningful tasks and receive trustworthy feedback. Scaling the learning algorithm matters, but scaling the quality and diversity of that experience matters enormously too.
